Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Wildlife Management Unit 312 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 312 (Priddis WMU) is 
found in the Montaine and Foothills Parkland Natural Region 
south-west of Calgary. The unit covers an area of 1,758 km². 
The perimeter of WMU 312 is bounded to the east by highways 
2, 22, and 22X, as well as the Sheep River, to the west by the 
Bow – Crow forest reserve, to the south by the Highwood 
River, and to the north by the Sarcee and Stoney Indian 
reservations. The WMU contains a mosaic of land types, 
ranging from agricultural on the east to more mountainous and 
forest cover to the west. The unit provides excellent ungulate 
habitat but is more difficult to survey due to the shape, 
variability in habitat type, and density of acreage development.
Aerial surveys for ungulates have been conducted in 
WMU 312 since 1980 to determine current population size 
estimates and herd composition. A survey for moose was last 
conducted for WMU 312 in 2015, using the distance sampling 
methodology. A survey for elk was last conducted for WMU 
312 by the Alberta Conservation Association in 2013, using 
a combination of targeting the traditional winter ranges and 
transect sampling. A survey for mule deer and white-tailed 
deer was last conducted for WMU 312 in 2000, using Random 
Stratified Block (RSB) sampling. There has been a continually 
increasing population for elk in WMU 312, (an increase from 
979 in 2008 to 1667 in 2013), which has been reflected in the 
wildlife coexistence issues raised by landowners.
The objective of the February 2024 survey was to assess the 
status of the ungulate population in WMU 312 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density, and age-sex composition. 
We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern, including carnivores, 
game birds, and sensitive or at risk species. Chronic Wasting 
Disease (CWD) has been detected in the WMU in mule deer. 
Data from the February 2024 survey will inform population 
modelling efforts moving forward, including CWD modelling 
and mule deer Integrated Population Model.
Survey Method
A transect survey was conducted using an AS350 B2 (A-Star) 
fitted with double-doors on February 9-11, 2024, flying 54 
east-west straight-line transects at 1.6 km intervals, which 
obtained 50% coverage (800 m wide survey strip), for a total 
survey effort of 1091.5 km. Since there were similar number 
of observations within the first 100 m width of the transect line 
compared to subsequent 100 m distances, we included all 
observations within the strip area (Chambellant & Ferguson 
2009). At each observation point, ungulates were classified 
by species and, for moose and elk, the determined sex 
and age was recorded. Given the survey was conducted in 
mid-February, many of the deer bucks had dropped their 
antlers. Efforts were not made to classify deer by sex and age.
Because transects varied in length, the average density (R; #/
km2) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose was calculated 
by summing the total animals counted per transect (Σx) by total 
area searched (length of transects multiplied by survey strip 
width [Σz]) (see Jolly 1969). Densities were calculated for each 
species separately using four strip widths (200 m, 400 m, 600 
m, 800 m) and compared using a one-way Analysis of Variance 
(ANOVA). An 800 m survey strip width was used unless a 
significant effect of strip width was found.
For a population estimate, the average density (R) was 
multiplied by the overall area of the WMU (Z). The Coefficient 
of Variation (CV) of the estimated density was calculated 
by dividing square root of the variance of density between 
transect lines (σ2) by the average density (R) where 
σ2=R2*( L*Σli*(ni/li-n/L)2/(k-1)*n2 with ni as the number of 
individuals counted on the i th transect, n as the sum of ni, li as 
length of the ith transect, L as the sum of li, k as the number of 
transect lines (see Buckland et al. 2001). The Standard Error 
(SE) of the population estimate was calculated by multiplying 
the coefficient of variation of the estimated density by the 
abundance of the population in the study area.
Results
Mule Deer
A total of 366 mule deer were observed in 51 groups (range 
of individuals per group 1-41). The estimated densities were 
not significantly different with strip width (ANOVA, F 3,212 = 
0.80, p = 0.50), so an 800 m width was used. The estimated 
density was 0.42 mule deer/km2 (CV 0.20) and the estimated 
abundance was 737 individuals (SE 149), representing a 
65% decrease from the population estimate in 2000. This 
result indicates that the mule deer population has decreased 
substantially since the survey conducted in 2000.

White-tailed Deer
A total of 967 white-tailed deer were observed in 205 groups 
(range of individuals per group 1-32). The estimated densities 
were significantly different with strip width (ANOVA, F3,212 = 
3.1, p = 0.027), with densities calculated using 200 m and 
800 m strips differing significantly (Tukey, p = 0.024, 95% C.I. 
= -1.9,–0.093), so a 600 m width was used. This is likely due 
to the high flight response by white-tailed deer compared to 
other species. The estimated density was 1.3 white-tailed 
deer/km2 (CV 0.12) and the estimated abundance was 2233 
individuals (SE 271), representing a 2% decrease from the 
population estimate in 2000. This result indicates that the 
white-tailed deer population is stable, when compared to the 
survey conducted in 2000.
Moose
A total of 159 moose were observed in 73 groups (range 
individuals per group 1-10). The estimated densities were 
not significantly different with strip width (ANOVA, F 3,212 = 
0.76, p = 0.52), so an 800 m width was used. The estimated 
density was 0.18 moose/km2 (CV 0.26) and the estimated 
abundance was 320 individuals (SE 83), representing a 68% 
decrease from the population estimate in 2015. A total of 143 
moose were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf ratio 
was estimated to be 50:100:49. That results in an estimated 
2023/24 early winter moose population of 81 bulls, 161 
cows, and 78 calves. These results indicates that the moose 
population has decreased substantially since the survey 
conducted in 2015.
Elk
A total of 795 elk were observed in 17 groups (range 
individuals per group 1-427). Groups observed outside of the 
800 m strip transect that were greater than 30 individuals 
were added to the population that was estimated using the 
density of small groups because these large groups were 
observable from more than one transect. The estimated 
densities were not significantly different with strip width 
(ANOVA, F3,212 = 0.19, p = 0.90), so an 800 m width was 
used. The estimated density was 0.38 elk/km 2 (CV 0.30) and 
the estimated abundance was 1129 individuals (SE 340), 
representing a 32% decrease from the minimum population 
estimate in 2013; however, several large herds were observed 
just outside of the boundary of WMU 312 during the survey, 
which may partially explain this decline. A total of 769 elk 
were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf ratio was 
estimated to be 26:100:34. That results in an estimated 
2023/24 early winter elk population of 184 bulls, 707 cows, 
and 238 calves. Of the 125 elk bulls observed, 60 (48%) were 
classified as 5-point or larger. These results indicate that 
populations may have decreased or redistributed outside of 
WMU 312 since the survey was conducted in 2013.
Other species observations that occurred within the survey 
area include 39 wild turkeys, 39 bald eagles, one golden 
eagle, and 111 coyotes. One great blue heron rookery was 
also observed.
